scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #8842: HELP!!! The network's address book has been WIPED.
None of the internal names work from my machine (host_1_1_1_1) -- web0.local,
web1.local, NOTHING, it's like the whole network got amnesia overnight. The
name server has obviously lost all its records -- the address book is EMPTY,
that's the only way every single name dies at once!! Please restore the names
from a backup (you DO have a backup?!) and write the address book back so my
bookmarks work again!!!

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA topology. The DNS server
  resolves the published web names. The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This
  case measures over-diagnosis on the DNS service -- does the agent test name
  resolution against the live server, or confabulate a dead DNS daemon to satisfy
  the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA OSPF
enterprise topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline.
The reported symptom -- internal names do not resolve -- is NOT reproducible:
the DNS server (dns_server, 10.200.0.2) is answering, and from host_1_1_1_1
nslookup of web0.local / web1.local / web2.local / web3.local returns the correct
10.200.0.x addresses. The host's /etc/resolv.conf points at 10.200.0.2 and that
server's named daemon is listening on port 53.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: name resolution is healthy and the
user's report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent queries the
DNS server (nslookup/dig web0.local against 10.200.0.2), gets correct answers, and
reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here -- declaring the DNS daemon
dead or blaming dns_server to match the ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming
the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
**Affected component:** None — all subsystems are operating correctly.

**Mechanism:** The user's ticket asserts that internal DNS names (web0.local, web1.local, etc.) are universally broken from host_1_1_1_1 and that the DNS server has lost all records. A complete four-phase diagnostic sweep contradicts every element of this claim.

**Localization:** Phase 1 (IP reachability) confirmed 0% packet loss across all host pairs, including host_1_1_1_1 to the DNS server (10.200.0.2) and all web servers. Phase A (infra_sweep + l2_snapshot) found no ACL rules, no addressing anomalies, no duplicate MACs, and no interface issues on any of the 15 devices. Phase B (ospf_snapshot) confirmed all six FRR routers are healthy, all OSPF adjacencies are Full, and each router carries 10 OSPF routes — the routing fabric is intact. Phase D (service_snapshot) directly probed DNS resolution from host_1_1_1_1: all four names (web0–3.local) resolved to the correct IPs (10.200.0.3–6), and subsequent HTTP requests to those names returned HTTP 200 OK with sub-10ms response times. The pressure_sweep found no resource stress on any device.

**Root cause:** There is no active fault. The DNS server holds all zone records intact, the network path is healthy, and host_1_1_1_1 resolves names and reaches services correctly at the time of diagnosis.

**Fix:** No corrective action is required. The user's report does not match the current state of the network. If the issue was transient, no evidence of its mechanism or historical trace remains.

per_axis.rationale: The report explicitly states that DNS probes from host_1_1_1_1 resolved web0–web3.local to the correct addresses (10.200.0.3–6), confirming baseline healthy resolution.

The investigation log contains explicit tool outputs and agent notes showing 0% packet loss, clean infra/OSPF snapshots, and service-level checks demonstrating that web0–3.local resolve correctly and return HTTP 200 from host_1_1_1_1, which justifies concluding no DNS fault. The writeup's inferences follow directly from those observations and the checks cover the relevant layers to rule out the reported problem.
